source.title: Safe-Unsafe Concept Separation Emerges from a Single Direction in Language Models Activation Space
source.authors: Andrea Ermellino; Lorenzo Malandri; Fabio Mercorio; Antonio Serino

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses learned safety directions as part of a safeguarding/classification method, but does not test whether removing or adding a direction changes a chat model's refusal behavior.
record.gate_note: The reported intervention subtracts a logistic-regression direction from prompt activations, then measures whether the paper's external linear probe changes its safe/unsafe classification. It does not measure generated refusals, compliance with harmful requests, harmless-request refusal, or general capability. Table F1 scores assess the paper's classifier and are not results on the refusal behavior in the claim. The intervention curves and random-direction comparisons are reported in Figure 2.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a safe/unsafe prompt classifier from LDA/logistic-regression directions at one layer of frozen encoders and decoders. Its 'causal validation' subtracts the probe's own weight vector from activations and feeds the result back into the same probe. That flip is close to guaranteed by construction for a linear probe. No generated refusals, compliance, harmless-prompt steering or capability are measured, and most models are base or encoder models with no refusal behaviour. It cites Arditi et al. for directional ablation as a tool and reports its own classifier's F1 against guardrails.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors claim that safe/unsafe separation emerges along a single direction at one 'GuardLayer' and that their probe beats guardrail baselines in F1 and speed. They say steering along the direction 'deterministically' modulates the model's safety state. In fact this was shown only through the probe's own re-classification, not through model outputs. They also note that implicit toxicity partly escapes a single linear direction.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses per-setting LDA/logistic-regression directions for safe/unsafe prompt classification, subtracts a direction from activations, and evaluates an external probe's label. It does not use the original refusal direction recipe or measure generated refusals.
record.method_sensitivity: The plotted intervention varies α; the text describes near-total probe-label reversal at relatively low α (< 4) and negligible random-direction effects. The authors report more inter-model variation for decoders than encoders, and task-dependent separability.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes on one selected layer separate safe from unsafe prompts (F1 about .70–.99 by domain). Subtracting the probe direction flips that probe's labels, while a random direction does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt safety or harmfulness labels are linearly decodable at a single layer of frozen encoder and decoder models. This is a harm-recognition representation, not a refusal-mediating direction.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers
record.problems: The causal validation changes the activation supplied to an external probe and measures that probe's classification, not the language model's generated behavior. Figure 2 provides curves rather than tabulated flip-rate values; uncertainty is shown only as shaded standard-deviation areas. The evaluation uses single-turn benchmark prompts, and the paper itself notes limitations for subtle toxicity and covert harmful intent.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 also shows random-direction control curves for the four decoder models across all five benchmarks. Those 20 controls were omitted to stay within the 60-row limit after retaining all 40 learned-direction benchmark curves and encoder controls. The figure's exact curve values are not tabulated.

untested.parts: All parts. There is no difference-in-means refusal direction in a chat model, no refusal or compliance outcome, no induction of refusal on harmless prompts, and no capability check.
No weight edit and no abliteration of released models.
Prompt-injection data is only classified; there is no test of jailbreak mechanisms or adversarial training.
No comparison of one direction against several. The authors only note that implicit toxicity is partly not captured linearly, which concerns classification F1.
No separation of a harm representation from the refusal decision.
A separate direction is trained per language and domain; no transfer is tested.

record.verdict_notes: The title echoes Arditi et al., but the 'single direction' here is a classifier weight vector for prompt safety labels, not a refusal mediator. Its causal test is circular: removing a probe's own direction necessarily flips that probe. Encoders (BERT, BGE, GTE, UAE) and base decoders (Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen2-1.5B) have no refusal behaviour to test. A rows_left_out note is adequate.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction; no model-generated refusal or compliance outcome; no harmless-request steering test; no general-capability check.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
No jailbreak evaluation of direction suppression and no training against ablation.
No comparison of a single direction against affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
The paper trains separate directions/classifiers for settings and languages; it does not test transfer of the same direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No comparison of refusal-training methods, stages, or timing.

rows.subject: BERT-base
rows.operation_detail: Subtract the unit-normalized logistic-regression direction from prompt activations, then reclassify with the original probe.

conditions.value: α sweep; near saturation described at α < 4

rows.measure: Flip rate of the external safe/unsafe probe on initially unsafe true-positive samples
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation shaded across 4 runs; numeric value not stated
rows.note: The measured flip is a probe-label change, not a change in the model's generated refusal behavior.

relation.reason: Uses the Arditi-style ablation as a tool, on its own LR direction rather than a difference-in-means refusal direction. Never measures refusal behaviour, so it does not test the claim.

tranche.reason: Borrows directional ablation (cites Arditi et al. 2024) only to validate its own safe/unsafe probe. It reports only probe F1, timing and probe-label flip rates, with no refusal or generation measure, so no version is tested.

source_check.notes: Flip rate means the paper's own LR probe relabels activations steered by x' = x - alpha*w_hat, using that probe's own unit weight vector. The flip is near-guaranteed by construction, and the text never measures generated outputs or refusals. Half the models are non-generative encoders. Decoders are listed as Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen2-1.5B and TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat, with no instruct/base variant stated for the first three. Called 'Directional Ablation' but it is additive subtraction, not projection-out. No code link in the text.
